The Integral Test

A series and an integral get stacked together and share one fate. The bars wrap the curve from above and below.

Stand bars under a decreasing curve, and the sum traps the integral from both sides. So the series and the integral converge or diverge together. An exponent above 1 gives convergence; anything else diverges. That fork decides the fate of every p-series.

For example, stack 📚 books like steps against a ramp. The steps dip below the ramp's curve and poke above it. Still, the steps' area and the area under the curve are finite together or endless together.

∫1N+1f≤∑n=1Nf(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1f\int_1^{N+1} f \le \sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n) \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} f∫1N+1​f≤n=1∑N​f(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1​f
∑1np converges  ⟺  p>1\sum \frac{1}{n^p} \text{ converges} \iff p > 1∑np1​ converges⟺p>1

    Since fff is decreasing, f(n+1)≤f(x)≤f(n)f(n+1) \le f(x) \le f(n)f(n+1)≤f(x)≤f(n) for x∈[n,n+1]x \in [n, n+1]x∈[n,n+1].

    Integrating over [n,n+1][n,n+1][n,n+1] (length 111) gives f(n+1)≤∫nn+1f≤f(n)f(n+1) \le \int_n^{n+1} f \le f(n)f(n+1)≤∫nn+1​f≤f(n) by monotonicity of the integral.

  2. Sum over n=1,…,Nn = 1, \ldots, Nn=1,…,N.

    The left inequalities sum to ∑n=1Nf(n+1)=∑k=2N+1f(k)≤∫1N+1f\sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n+1) = \sum_{k=2}^{N+1} f(k) \le \int_1^{N+1} f∑n=1N​f(n+1)=∑k=2N+1​f(k)≤∫1N+1​f; the right ones to ∫1N+1f≤∑n=1Nf(n)\int_1^{N+1} f \le \sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n)∫1N+1​f≤∑n=1N​f(n).

    With SN=∑n=1Nf(n)S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n)SN​=∑n=1N​f(n), the correct identity is ∑k=2N+1f(k)=SN+1−f(1)=SN−f(1)+f(N+1)\sum_{k=2}^{N+1} f(k) = S_{N+1} - f(1) = S_N - f(1) + f(N+1)∑k=2N+1​f(k)=SN+1​−f(1)=SN​−f(1)+f(N+1).

    Hence the left side gives SN+1−f(1)≤∫1N+1fS_{N+1} - f(1) \le \int_1^{N+1} fSN+1​−f(1)≤∫1N+1​f, i.e. SN+1≤f(1)+∫1N+1fS_{N+1} \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} fSN+1​≤f(1)+∫1N+1​f, and since f>0f > 0f>0, SN≤SN+1S_N \le S_{N+1}SN​≤SN+1​, so SN≤f(1)+∫1N+1fS_N \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} fSN​≤f(1)+∫1N+1​f as well.

    Chaining with the right side gives ∫1N+1f≤∑n=1Nf(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1f\int_1^{N+1} f \le \sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n) \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} f∫1N+1​f≤∑n=1N​f(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1​f.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow)(⇐) If ∫1∞f\int_1^{\infty} f∫1∞​f converges (i.e. ∫1Rf\int_1^{R} f∫1R​f has a finite limit as R→∞R \to \inftyR→∞), then the partial sums ∑n=1Nf(n)\sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n)∑n=1N​f(n) are bounded above by f(1)+∫1∞ff(1) + \int_1^{\infty} ff(1)+∫1∞​f and, the terms being nonnegative, converge by the monotone convergence theorem.

    Passing to the limit preserves the inequalities: ∫N+1∞f≤RN≤∫N∞f\int_{N+1}^{\infty} f \le R_N \le \int_{N}^{\infty} f∫N+1∞​f≤RN​≤∫N∞​f.
